I think you are really on to something here. I would just add that the digitization of media and the difficulty in consistently monetizing media are both huge factors to consider. These two concepts would generally fit your timeframe of the last 10 years. Not that everything occurred in the last 10 years, more so that the pace of change quickened.

Something else that gave rise to this balkanization of media choices is when we in the US went from 3 broadcast channels to 1000 cable channels. This opened up possibilities to people that you could have a channel devoted entirely to golf or nature or Ax Men or whatever. Ok, I just had an idea for a really bad TV show - Axe Men - a show about guys who wear too much Axe Body spray. In any event, these 1000+ cable channels were still created and ran as media companies, whether stand alone or as part of a larger existing network (i.e. CNBC). They differ from where we are today with the countless iterations of Joe Schmo and his blog and pony show. However, those 1000 plus cable channels planted the seed in Joe Schmo's mind that he could do his own thing. Although yes, this can easily lead to echo chambers, I think this is just a side-effect of Joe Schmo wanting to have his say.

Because media is increasingly consumed globally (as opposed to primarily the US), movies are becoming more common (shallow) in their form and content. The movie concentrates more on the car chase or exploding building or superhero, which translates more readily across cultures and continents as opposed to witty dialogue that might be laced with slang or regional dialects or otherwise be hard for a non-native speaker to truly appreciate. Call this the Michael Bey model. This model still works to an extent, but the explosion of content creators (the microbrewers of media) is filling the voids left by the monolithic movies. I would think movie studios are doing whatever they can to make their money in movie theaters as opposed to elsewhere, as I would think it would be easier to collect the money in a theater as opposed to thousands of home computers. That is partly why I think we are seeing a greater emphasis on 3-D and IMAX and any number of technologies that add more to the theater experience compared to the at home on your couch experience. This paragraph is mostly hypothesis on my part - I generally stay away from movies theaters.

For a historical comparison, the variety of countries producing movies greatly declined at the development of sound in the late 1920s / early 1930s. A silent movie relied more on action and less on dialogue, which allowed a movie produced in one country to be able to be shown around the world. Once sound came along, movies were primarily produced in English. This was a competitive advantage for Hollywood and a loss of a huge market for non-English speaking countries producing movies. You could probably say that movies became more homogenized once sound was added to movie pictures.

Were we go from here is anyone's guess. When professional athletes go on strike, it is usually a contest of billionaires (owners) versus millionaires (athletes). Not surprisingly, the billionaires usually win. Regarding media, while my brain says bet on the billionaires (big media companies), my gut says Joe Schmo's blog is isn't going anywhere.
